description:
Guys Reach out to me on my email, please

Hey, I’m Mohammad, an Engineering I student at McMaster from India, previously at BITS Pilani, Goa. I’m interested in space exploration and engineering, and I’m putting together a team to identify Earth locations that could serve as analogues for permanent Moon and Mars bases. We’ll research potential sites, study their environments, and explore the challenges of building future extraterrestrial settlements!
summary: Early crews on Mars will need shelter from radiation, large temperature swings, and micrometeorites. Lava tubes and other caves provide all three, but robots lose communication and sunlight inside them, so the technology to explore caves must be tested on Earth first. We screened the 1,062 candidates in the USGS Mars Global Cave Candidate Catalog and found that 84% sit in the Tharsis volcanic region, where landing is hardest. We then compared 11 sites on landing elevation, cave evidence, ice access, and solar power. In our preliminary ranking, lower-elevation sites in Arabia Terra and the Kasei Valles area outscored the famous Tharsis skylights because they are far easier to land at, but they have weaker evidence of true lava tubes. Confirming caves at such sites is the gap this work highlights. We matched the top sites to Earth analogs where cave-exploration technology can be tested. The best matches are Umm Jirsan (Saudi Arabia) for Daedalia Planum and the Corona lava tube (Lanzarote, Spain) for Arsia Mons.
details: Caves are the most promising early habitat on Mars, but the best documented ones sit where landing is hardest, the sites with ice and easy landing are poorly checked for caves, and the technology to explore caves has not been tested in matching terrain. Though earth cannot reproduce Mars gravity, atmosphere, or radiation, it can reproduce cave geometry, rock type, and the robotic problems of working without line of sight, power, or communication. Our project intends to address this by defining what an early human base needs from a cave site, screening known Mars cave candidates against those needs using NASA and USGS data, and matching top sites to Earth analogs and state where each analogy breaks down. We used two groups, lava tubes (group A), matching the volcanic Mars sites (Jovis Tholus, Daedalia Planum, Arsia Mons) and cave-like fractures and collapse pits in cold, non-volcanic terrain, matching Arabia Terra, Kasei Valles, and NE of Kasei (group B). Ultimately, the screening conducted points to a clear gap. The best-documented Mars caves are on high volcanic terrain that is hard to land at, while low-elevation sites at ice-bearing latitudes have weaker cave evidence. The next step is to confirm voids at the top low-elevation sites using high-resolution imaging and orbital radar, then to test cave-exploration technology (relay communication, mapping, and tethered mobility) at the matched Earth analogs: Corona Lava Tubes and Umm Jirsan Caves.
